_comment: Two budgets in SI seconds, never netted against each other. Cost and latency are opposed --
batching buys one with the other -- so a cost improvement may not license a latency
regression, and seconds/ratchet.py keeps them as two independent floors.
THERE ARE NO FLOORS YET, AND THAT IS THE POINT. This file previously recorded 1.195s of
latency and 0.184s of cost, measured on a live endpoint whose interactor had no engine: every
job was answered by the gate or by the missing-weights error. Those were floors on a path
that decomposed nothing, which is the worst kind of gate -- green, precise, and measuring the
absence of the work. Gall's law runs the other way: a ratchet starts from a simple system
that works, and there was none to start from.
There is one now, in `working` below. A floor may be recorded once the working system has
been measured MIN_SAMPLES times through the interactor, and not before -- one run is an
anecdote, and the ratchet judges against a spread.
The simple system that works, and the thing every later number must be compared against.
It is upstream's pipeline run directly, with no transport layer, no bus and no interactor
in the picture -- so a regression after this is ours.

weights._comment: The same volume. A pod mounts it at its volumeMountPath and a serverless worker at /runpod-volume, so HF_HOME differs between the two for one set of bytes.

run.output: test.psd, 8476354 bytes, 9 named layers with per-layer bounds; test_depth.psd beside it
run._seconds_note: The program's own number for the final stage, not a clock kept outside it. Denoising ran 30 steps at about 1.57 s/step. One run: evidence that it works, not a distribution.

latency_seconds.what: One decomposition, end to end as the caller sees it: queue delay plus execution.

cost_seconds.what: Billed GPU seconds for one decomposition: RunPod executionTime, what the endpoint charges.
